posts.text: It’s not perfect but you get the idea. Despite prices rising, mining investment (capex) is still lagging what’s needed to replace production. During the early 2000’s there was a lot of cheque writing by mining fund managers. (I worked at a major one) Today investment flows are largely ETF’s and they don’t write cheques and cash up mining companies. The industry has become conservative with expenditures. At some point this will all change. But I don’t see it happening until commodity prices are much higher and there’s certainty on capex payback. Business / economy uncertainty is a killer for investment. It’s a difficult climate and today’s big commodity consumers are avoiding vertical integration and instead sitting back and expecting someone else to fund the industry. Question is… who will that somebody be? Actively managed mining funds ain’t what they used to be… today’s youthful investors are more interested in ramping funds in and out of ETF’s like COPX than just parking money with a manager that will actually fund mining exploration and production.

posts.text: Just bc something is held as a “reserve” by CBs does not mean it is “money”. Bonds are not money. They may be “money like” but they are not money. If they were money they would not have to be sold or pledged to get liquidity when money was needed. Same goes for Oil and for Gold.

posts.text: Demand for Chinese chips is skyrocketing: Chinese integrated circuit industry revenue jumped +22% YoY in 2025, to a record $245 billion. Since 2020, Chinese chip industry sales have nearly doubled. As a result, China now accounts for ~6% of the global semiconductor market. This is roughly in-line with Japan and the European Union, at ~7% each, and Taiwan, at ~6%. By comparison, North America represents 53% of the market, while South Korea accounts for 21%. China is rapidly emerging as a major global player in semiconductors.

posts.text: BREAKING: China's net new loans dropped -$50.4 billion in July, marking only the 3rd monthly decline this century. This is a broad measure of new bank lending in China and a key gauge of overall economic activity. The decline was also more than 3x larger than expected. Loans extended specifically to the real economy posted an even sharper drop, with net repayments of -$87.5 billion, the largest monthly decline in data going back to 2002. Aggregate financing, a broader measure of total credit, rose +$207.7 billion, but almost all of it came from +$192.9 billion in government bond sales rather than organic private lending. This comes as corporate and household longer-term loans shrank, reflecting weak investment appetite and demand for property. China's economic activity is deteriorating sharply.
